\chapter{Family}
\label{ch:pt-family}
\hlchaptermodality{10}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name my parents and my siblings in Portuguese and say why irmão is not built on Latin's frater.}

Say o pai, a mãe, o irmão, a irmã with their nasal endings, then cut frāter germānus down to germānus alone and land on irmão, twin of Spanish hermano.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[o pai, a mãe]{o pai, a mãe — the family words worn to the bone}

\label{lesson:PT-C10-pais}



\begin{quote}
Every Romance sister descends from \emph{pater} and \emph{māter}, but \textbf{Portuguese wore them down the furthest}. Italian kept \emph{padre/madre}; French \emph{père/mère}; Portuguese dissolved the middle consonant entirely, leaving the one-syllable \textbf{pai} and the nasal \textbf{mãe}.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{o pai} (\textquotedblleft{}father\textquotedblright{}) $\leftarrow$ Latin \textbf{pater}. Portuguese dropped the intervocalic \textbf{-t-} completely: \emph{pater $\to$ pae $\to$ pai}. The same disappearing-\emph{-t-} you saw in Ch.1's \emph{noite} is here taken all the way to a bare diphthong.
  \item \textbf{a mãe} (\textquotedblleft{}mother\textquotedblright{}) $\leftarrow$ Latin \textbf{māter}. Same loss of \emph{-t-}, and the \emph{a} soaked up a nasal from the lost \emph{-n-}/\emph{-m-} environment $\to$ the tilde vowel \textbf{ã} (\emph{mãe} = \textquotedblleft{}mahng-ee,\textquotedblright{} nasal).
\end{itemize}

Articles: \emph{o} pai (masculine), \emph{a} mãe (feminine).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: The plural trick — os pais}]
Portuguese says \textbf{os pais} for \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{the parents}\textquotedblright{} — but literally it is \textquotedblleft{}the \textbf{fathers}.\textquotedblright{} Like Spanish \emph{los padres}, the masculine plural \textbf{covers a mixed group}: one father + one mother = \emph{os pais}. (And mind the spelling twin: \textbf{o país} — with an accent — means \textquotedblleft{}the \textbf{country}\textquotedblright{}; \emph{os pais} / \emph{os países} are a classic pair to keep straight.)

The learned adjectives, borrowed back from Latin, still show the old root: \textbf{pat}ernal, \textbf{mat}ernal — so \emph{pai} and \emph{paternal} are the worn-down and the dressed-up versions of the same word.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}o pai, a mãe\textquotedblright{} — \emph{mãe} fully nasal
  \item the erosion — \textquotedblleft{}\emph{pater} $\to$ \emph{pae} $\to$ \textbf{pai}; the \emph{-t-} vanished\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}os pais = the parents (lit. 'the fathers'); mind \emph{o país} = country\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give \textquotedblleft{}father\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}mother\textquotedblright{} with articles. (\textbf{o pai, a mãe}.) What happened to the \emph{-t-} of \emph{pater/māter} in Portuguese? (It \textbf{vanished} — \emph{pater $\to$ pae $\to$ pai}.) What does \textbf{os pais} mean literally and in use? (Literally \textquotedblleft{}the fathers\textquotedblright{}; in use, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{the parents}.\textquotedblright{}) What word does \emph{o país} (accented) mean? (The \textbf{country} — a spelling trap.) Next: \textbf{o irmão, a irmã} — and a surprise about where \textquotedblleft{}brother\textquotedblright{} comes from.

\section[o irmão, a irmã]{o irmão, a irmã — the brother who isn't a \textquotedblleft{}frater\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:PT-C10-irmaos}



\begin{quote}
French and Italian build \textquotedblleft{}brother\textquotedblright{} from Latin \emph{frāter} (\emph{frère}, \emph{fratello}). Portuguese — and Spanish with it — does something completely different, and it is one of the best etymologies in the whole language.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{o irmão} (\textquotedblleft{}brother\textquotedblright{}) and \textbf{a irmã} (\textquotedblleft{}sister\textquotedblright{}) come \textbf{not} from \emph{frāter} but from Latin \textbf{germānus}, meaning \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{genuine, of the same stock, born of the same parents.}\textquotedblright{}
  \item The Romans said \textbf{frāter germānus} — a \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{full} brother,\textquotedblright{} one sharing both parents, as opposed to a half-brother. Over time Iberian speakers \textbf{dropped the \emph{frāter}} and kept the adjective: \emph{(frāter) germānus $\to$ irmão}. So a Portuguese brother is literally a \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{full-blood} one.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

Articles: \emph{o} irmão (masc.), \emph{a} irmã (fem.); the masculine plural \textbf{os irmãos} covers a mixed set (\textquotedblleft{}siblings\textquotedblright{}), exactly as \emph{os pais} did for parents.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{cousinweb}
That same \emph{germānus} \textquotedblleft{}of the same stock\textquotedblright{} fans out in English:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{germane} — \textquotedblleft{}relevant, closely related\textquotedblright{} (originally \textquotedblleft{}having the same parents\textquotedblright{}).
  \item \textbf{German} — the \textbf{people-name}! The Romans called the tribes across the Rhine \emph{Germani}, plausibly \textquotedblleft{}the genuine/kindred ones.\textquotedblright{} So \emph{irmão} (\textquotedblleft{}brother\textquotedblright{}) and \emph{German} (the nation) spring from one Latin word for \textbf{kinship}.
\end{itemize}

Spanish made the \textbf{identical} swap — \emph{hermano / hermana} — so Portuguese \emph{irmão} and Spanish \emph{hermano} are twins, both meaning \textquotedblleft{}full-blood brother,\textquotedblright{} both leaving \emph{frāter} behind (kept only in bookish \emph{fraternal / fraterno}).
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}o irmão, a irmã\textquotedblright{} — both nasal endings
  \item the origin — \textquotedblleft{}\emph{frāter germānus} $\to$ drop \emph{frāter} $\to$ \textbf{irmão}, 'full brother'\textquotedblright{}
  \item the cousins — \textquotedblleft{}germano $\to$ germane, and \emph{German} the people\textquotedblright{}
  \item the twin — \textquotedblleft{}Portuguese \emph{irmão} = Spanish \emph{hermano}\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give \textquotedblleft{}brother\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}sister\textquotedblright{} with articles. (\textbf{o irmão, a irmã}.) What Latin word are they from — and what did it mean? (\textbf{germānus} — \textquotedblleft{}genuine, of the same parents\textquotedblright{}; from \emph{frāter germānus}, \textquotedblleft{}full brother.\textquotedblright{}) Name two English cousins of \emph{germānus}. (\textbf{germane}; \textbf{German}, the people-name.) What is the Spanish twin of \emph{irmão}? (\emph{hermano}.) Next chapter: sentences about the whole family.
